lessons.title: Lesson 1: Costing Fundamentals for Water Tank Projects in Africa
lessons.body: Every water tank project in Africa lives or dies by the numbers. Before you mix a single bag of cement or lay a single brick, you must know your costs to the shilling, naira, rand, or cedi. This lesson gives you the costing framework that separates profitable contractors from those who finish a job and wonder where the money went. We will use a 10,000-litre tank as our working example, because that is the sweet spot for most households, schools, and small businesses across the continent. Start with the three cost pillars: materials, labour, and overheads. Materials typically consume 55 to 65 percent of your budget. Labour takes 20 to 30 percent. Overheads, transport, and contingency eat the rest. If your materials are above 70 percent, you are probably over-specifying. If labour is above 35 percent, your crew is inefficient or you are paying for skills you do not need. Let us break down a 10,000-litre ferrocement tank in Kenya, using KES. Cement: 25 bags at KES 750 each equals KES 18,750. Sand: 3 tonnes at KES 2,500 per tonne equals KES 7,500. Ballast or murram for the base: 2 tonnes at KES 1,800 equals KES 3,600. Chicken mesh or wire mesh: 8 rolls at KES 1,200 equals KES 9,600. Reinforcement bars, 12mm: 20 lengths at KES 850 equals KES 17,000. Binding wire: 5 kg at KES 250 equals KES 1,250. Waterproofing admixture: 2 litres at KES 1,500 equals KES 3,000. PVC inlet, outlet, overflow, and washout fittings: KES 4,500. Tap and standpipe: KES 2,000. Labour: 4 masons for 6 days at KES 1,200 per day equals KES 28,800. 2 helpers for 6 days at KES 700 equals KES 8,400. Total direct cost: KES 104,400. Add 10 percent contingency: KES 10,440. Add transport and miscellaneous: KES 8,000. Your floor price is KES 122,840. Your selling price should be 25 to 35 percent above that. At 30 percent markup, you quote KES 159,692, round to KES 160,000. That is KES 16 per litre of storage. In Nigeria, a similar 10,000-litre concrete tank in NGN: cement 30 bags at NGN 8,500 equals NGN 255,000. Sand 4 tonnes at NGN 25,000 equals NGN 100,000. Granite 3 tonnes at NGN 45,000 equals NGN 135,000. Reinforcement 25 lengths at NGN 9,000 equals NGN 225,000. Mesh 10 rolls at NGN 15,000 equals NGN 150,000. Fittings and waterproofing: NGN 80,000. Labour: 5 masons for 7 days at NGN 8,000 equals NGN 280,000. 3 helpers for 7 days at NGN 4,000 equals NGN 84,000. Total direct: NGN 1,309,000. Contingency 10 percent: NGN 130,900. Transport and misc: NGN 70,000. Floor price: NGN 1,509,900. Markup 30 percent: NGN 1,962,870, round to NGN 1,960,000. That is NGN 196 per litre. In South Africa, a 10,000-litre plastic rotational-moulded tank retails between ZAR 12,000 and ZAR 18,000 depending on thickness and UV rating. A brick tank of the same capacity in ZAR: bricks 2,500 at ZAR 3.50 equals ZAR 8,750. Cement 20 bags at ZAR 110 equals ZAR 2,200. Sand 3 tonnes at ZAR 450 equals ZAR 1,350. Stone 2 tonnes at ZAR 600 equals ZAR 1,200. Reinforcement 15 lengths at ZAR 180 equals ZAR 2,700. Waterproofing and fittings: ZAR 3,500. Labour: 3 masons for 8 days at ZAR 450 per day equals ZAR 10,800. 2 helpers for 8 days at ZAR 300 equals ZAR 4,800. Total direct: ZAR 35,300. Contingency 10 percent: ZAR 3,530. Transport: ZAR 2,500. Floor price: ZAR 41,330. Markup 30 percent: ZAR 53,729, round to ZAR 54,000. That is ZAR 5.40 per litre. In Ghana, a 10,000-litre ferrocement tank in GHS: cement 25 bags at GHS 60 equals GHS 1,500. Sand 3 tonnes at GHS 200 equals GHS 600. Mesh 8 rolls at GHS 100 equals GHS 800. Reinforcement 20 lengths at GHS 70 equals GHS 1,400. Fittings and waterproofing: GHS 500. Labour: 4 masons for 6 days at GHS 100 equals GHS 2,400. 2 helpers for 6 days at GHS 60 equals GHS 720. Total direct: GHS 7,920. Contingency 10 percent: GHS 792. Transport: GHS 600. Floor price: GHS 9,312. Markup 30 percent: GHS 12,106, round to GHS 12,000. That is GHS 1.20 per litre. Notice the pattern: plastic tanks are cheapest per litre at scale, but they cannot be built on site in remote areas, they degrade under intense UV unless stabilised, and they cannot be repaired easily. Ferrocement and concrete tanks cost more upfront but last 30 to 50 years with minimal maintenance. Brick tanks sit in between. Your costing must account for site access. If a lorry cannot reach the site, you pay for head-loading or donkey transport, which can add 15 to 25 percent to material costs. Always visit the site before quoting. Measure the distance from the nearest motorable road. Check water availability for curing. Check if sand and aggregate are locally available or must be trucked in. A tank built 50 km from a quarry will cost more than one built next door. Labour rates vary by region and season. During planting season, unskilled labour is scarce and expensive. During dry season, it is abundant and cheap. Plan your projects around these cycles. Safety note: never let workers handle cement without dust masks and gloves. Cement burns are common and serious. Provide clean drinking water on site. Keep a basic first aid kit with burn gel and eye wash. Your costing must include PPE: helmets, boots, gloves, masks, and reflective vests. Budget KES 500 per worker per project in Kenya, NGN 3,000 in Nigeria, ZAR 300 in South Africa, GHS 50 in Ghana. Do not skip this. A single injury can wipe out your profit and your reputation. Finally, always quote in writing. Include a validity period of 14 to 30 days because material prices fluctuate. Include a payment schedule: 50 percent deposit, 30 percent at wall completion, 20 percent on handover. Never start work without a deposit. That deposit buys your materials and protects you from clients who change their minds. Your costing is your business plan. Master it, and you will build tanks that pay you well.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Material Selection and Procurement for African Water Tanks
lessons.body: Choosing the right material for a water tank in Africa is not about picking the cheapest option. It is about matching the material to the site, the budget, the water quality, and the lifespan you promise your client. This lesson walks through ferrocement, concrete, plastic, and brick tanks, with real procurement numbers from Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, and Ghana. Ferrocement is the most versatile option for rural and peri-urban Africa. You need cement, sand, wire mesh, reinforcement bars, and waterproofing admixture. The mesh is the skeleton. Use galvanised chicken mesh with 12mm to 25mm openings, or welded wire mesh with 50mm by 50mm openings. In Kenya, a 90-metre roll of chicken mesh costs KES 1,200. In Nigeria, a 30-metre roll of welded mesh costs NGN 15,000. In South Africa, a 30-metre roll of galvanised mesh costs ZAR 450. In Ghana, a 30-metre roll costs GHS 100. Buy mesh in bulk from hardware suppliers or directly from manufacturers. Avoid rusty mesh. Rust weakens the bond with cement and shortens tank life. Cement must be fresh. Check the date on the bag. Cement older than three months loses strength. In Kenya, Bamburi or Mombasa Cement 50kg bags cost KES 750. In Nigeria, Dangote or BUA 50kg bags cost NGN 8,500. In South Africa, PPC or AfriSam 50kg bags cost ZAR 110. In Ghana, Ghacem or Dangote 50kg bags cost GHS 60. Store cement on wooden pallets in a dry room. Never store it on a bare floor. Moisture ruins it. Sand must be clean, sharp, and free of silt and clay. Test it by putting a handful in a bottle of water. Shake it. If the water turns muddy, the sand has too much silt. Wash it or find another source. River sand is best. Pit sand often has clay. In Kenya, river sand costs KES 2,500 per tonne delivered. In Nigeria, sharp sand costs NGN 25,000 per tonne. In South Africa, river sand costs ZAR 450 per tonne. In Ghana, river sand costs GHS 200 per tonne. Reinforcement bars, commonly called rebar, come in 6mm, 8mm, 10mm, 12mm, and 16mm diameters. For a 10,000-litre tank, use 10mm or 12mm bars for the ring beam and vertical supports. In Kenya, a 12-metre length of 12mm rebar costs KES 850. In Nigeria, it costs NGN 9,000. In South Africa, it costs ZAR 180. In Ghana, it costs GHS 70. Buy from reputable dealers. Fake rebar is common. Test by cutting a small piece and bending it. Good rebar bends without cracking. Waterproofing admixture is essential for concrete and ferrocement tanks. It fills the pores in the cement matrix and stops water seepage. Use a crystalline waterproofing product or a liquid polymer admixture. In Kenya, 2 litres cost KES 1,500. In Nigeria, 5 litres cost NGN 12,000. In South Africa, 5 litres cost ZAR 350. In Ghana, 5 litres cost GHS 150. Do not substitute with ordinary paint. Paint peels and contaminates water. Concrete tanks use cement, sand, granite or ballast, rebar, and waterproofing. They are strong and durable but heavy. You need a solid foundation and good formwork. Formwork timber or steel must be rented or bought. In Kenya, formwork rental for a 10,000-litre tank costs KES 15,000 for two weeks. In Nigeria, it costs NGN 80,000. In South Africa, it costs ZAR 2,000. In Ghana, it costs GHS 800. Plastic tanks are factory-made from polyethylene or polypropylene. They are cheap, quick to install, and easy to clean. But they have limits. They degrade under UV light unless treated with carbon black or UV stabilisers. They crack if dropped or hit. They cannot be repaired easily. They are not suitable for very hot water or for sites with extreme temperature swings. In Kenya, a 10,000-litre plastic tank costs KES 85,000 to KES 120,000. In Nigeria, it costs NGN 800,000 to NGN 1,200,000. In South Africa, it costs ZAR 12,000 to ZAR 18,000. In Ghana, it costs GHS 3,000 to GHS 5,000. Buy from manufacturers with a warranty of at least 5 years. Check the wall thickness. Thicker is better. A 10,000-litre tank should have at least 5mm wall thickness. Brick tanks are built from burnt clay bricks, cement mortar, and a waterproof render. They are popular in South Africa and Zimbabwe. Bricks are strong, fire-resistant, and locally available. But they are labour-intensive and require skilled bricklayers. In South Africa, a brick costs ZAR 3.50. In Kenya, a brick costs KES 25. In Nigeria, a brick costs NGN 150. In Ghana, a brick costs GHS 2. You need about 2,500 bricks for a 10,000-litre tank. Procurement strategy: buy in bulk to get discounts. A 10 percent discount on materials is a 10 percent increase in profit. Negotiate with suppliers. Build relationships. Pay on time. Ask for credit terms if you have a track record. For remote sites, buy everything at once and transport it together. Split deliveries cost more. Use a pickup or lorry with a tarpaulin cover. Rain ruins cement and mesh. Safety note: when handling rebar, wear gloves. Cut ends are sharp. When mixing cement, wear a dust mask. When working at height, use scaffolding, not ladders. Ladders slip. Scaffolding with guardrails is safer. Store materials securely. Theft is a real risk. Lock cement and rebar in a container or store room. Insure your materials if the project is large. Finally, keep a materials log. Record every bag of cement, every roll of mesh, every length of rebar. Compare actual usage to your estimate. If you use more than planned, find out why. Maybe your mix was too wet. Maybe your mesh was cut inefficiently. Learn from every project. Your material selection and procurement skills are the backbone of your tank business.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Labour, Pricing, and Client Negotiation in African Water Tank Business
lessons.body: You can have the best materials and the best design, but if you cannot manage labour and price your work correctly, you will not stay in business. This lesson focuses on the people side of tank construction and the money side of client relationships. Start with labour. A typical tank crew has masons, helpers, and a foreman. For a 10,000-litre ferrocement tank, you need 4 masons and 2 helpers for 6 days. For a concrete tank, you need 5 masons and 3 helpers for 7 days. For a brick tank, you need 3 masons and 2 helpers for 8 days. For a plastic tank, you need 2 installers for 1 day. In Kenya, a mason earns KES 1,200 per day. A helper earns KES 700. A foreman earns KES 1,800. In Nigeria, a mason earns NGN 8,000. A helper earns NGN 4,000. A foreman earns NGN 12,000. In South Africa, a mason earns ZAR 450. A helper earns ZAR 300. A foreman earns ZAR 600. In Ghana, a mason earns GHS 100. A helper earns GHS 60. A foreman earns GHS 150. These rates vary by city and by season. In Nairobi, Mombasa, Lagos, Abuja, Johannesburg, Cape Town, Accra, and Kumasi, rates are higher. In rural areas, they are lower. Pay your workers on time. Pay them fairly. A hungry crew is a slow crew. A resentful crew steals or sabotages. Provide lunch or a lunch allowance. In Kenya, budget KES 200 per worker per day for lunch. In Nigeria, NGN 1,500. In South Africa, ZAR 80. In Ghana, GHS 20. This small cost buys loyalty and productivity. Train your helpers. A helper who can mix cement correctly, cut mesh, and tie rebar is worth more than a helper who only carries water. Promote from within. Your best mason today was your best helper yesterday. Safety on site is non-negotiable. Provide helmets, boots, gloves, and dust masks. In Kenya, a basic PPE kit costs KES 2,500 per worker. In Nigeria, NGN 15,000. In South Africa, ZAR 500. In Ghana, GHS 250. This is a one-time cost per worker if they keep their gear. Deduct from wages if they lose it. Enforce safety rules. No sandals on site. No drinking alcohol during work. No working at height without a harness. A fall from a 2-metre tank wall can kill. Now pricing. Your price must cover materials, labour, overheads, contingency, and profit. Use the formula: Price equals Direct Costs plus Overheads plus Contingency plus Profit. Direct costs are materials and labour. Overheads are transport, tools, insurance, and administration. Contingency is 10 percent of direct costs. Profit is 20 to 35 percent of total costs. Let us price a 10,000-litre ferrocement tank in Kenya. Direct costs: KES 104,400. Overheads: KES 8,000. Contingency: KES 10,440. Subtotal: KES 122,840. Profit at 30 percent: KES 36,852. Price: KES 159,692. Round to KES 160,000. In Nigeria, direct costs: NGN 1,309,000. Overheads: NGN 70,000. Contingency: NGN 130,900. Subtotal: NGN 1,509,900. Profit at 30 percent: NGN 452,970. Price: NGN 1,962,870. Round to NGN 1,960,000. In South Africa, direct costs: ZAR 35,300. Overheads: ZAR 2,500. Contingency: ZAR 3,530. Subtotal: ZAR 41,330. Profit at 30 percent: ZAR 12,399. Price: ZAR 53,729. Round to ZAR 54,000. In Ghana, direct costs: GHS 7,920. Overheads: GHS 600. Contingency: GHS 792. Subtotal: GHS 9,312. Profit at 30 percent: GHS 2,794. Price: GHS 12,106. Round to GHS 12,000. Client negotiation is where you win or lose. Never negotiate on price alone. Negotiate on scope. If the client says your price is too high, ask what they can remove. Maybe they can do the excavation themselves. Maybe they can provide water for curing. Maybe they can wait until dry season when labour is cheaper. Offer a smaller tank. A 5,000-litre tank costs about 60 percent of a 10,000-litre tank, not 50 percent, because fixed costs like mobilisation and formwork do not halve. Explain the difference between your tank and a cheap plastic tank. Your tank lasts 30 years. A plastic tank lasts 10 years if it is not damaged. Your tank can be repaired. A plastic tank cannot. Your tank adds value to the property. A plastic tank is temporary. Always quote in writing. Include a scope of work, a bill of quantities, a payment schedule, and a timeline. Include a warranty: 5 years on workmanship, 1 year on fittings. Include a clause for price adjustment if material prices rise more than 10 percent before the project starts. Get a signed contract. A handshake is not enough. For large projects, ask for a deposit of 50 percent. For small projects, ask for 70 percent. Never buy materials with your own money unless you have a signed contract and a deposit. If the client refuses a deposit, walk away. That client will not pay on time. Build a referral network. Happy clients tell their neighbours. In rural Africa, word of mouth is the best marketing. Give a small discount to the first client in a village. Use that project as a showpiece. Take photos. Put them on WhatsApp and Facebook. Print a simple brochure. Include your phone number. Follow up with past clients after one year. Ask if the tank is working well. Ask for referrals. Offer a maintenance service. Check the tank, clean the gutters, repair minor cracks. Charge a small fee. This recurring revenue keeps your business alive between big projects. Finally, keep records. Every project should have a file: contract, receipts, photos, client contact, profit and loss. Review your records every three months. Which projects made money? Which lost money? Why? Adjust your pricing and your process. Your business is not just building tanks. It is building trust, reputation, and profit. Master labour and negotiation, and you will build all three.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Business Systems, Record Keeping, and Scaling Your Water Tank Enterprise
lessons.body: You have built a few tanks. You have made some money. Now you want to grow. Growth requires systems. Without systems, you will stay small, stressed, and broke. This lesson gives you the business systems that turn a one-man crew into a tank-building enterprise. Start with record keeping. You need three books: a cash book, a project ledger, and a materials inventory. The cash book records every shilling, naira, rand, or cedi that comes in and goes out. Date, description, amount in, amount out, balance. Write it down the same day. Do not wait until the end of the week. You will forget. The project ledger records every cost and every payment for each project. Client name, location, tank type, capacity, start date, end date, materials cost, labour cost, transport cost, other costs, total cost, contract price, profit. This tells you which projects are profitable. The materials inventory records what you have in stock. Cement bags, mesh rolls, rebar lengths, fittings. When you buy, add to inventory. When you use, subtract. When you count, reconcile. This stops theft and waste. Use a simple notebook or a spreadsheet on your phone. In Kenya, you can use Excel on a laptop or Google Sheets on a phone. In Nigeria, use a notebook from a stationery shop. In South Africa, use a bookkeeping app. In Ghana, use a simple ledger book. The tool does not matter. The habit matters. Separate your business money from your personal money. Open a business bank account or a mobile money account. In Kenya, use M-Pesa or a bank account. In Nigeria, use a bank account or Opay. In South Africa, use a bank account or Capitec. In Ghana, use MTN Mobile Money or a bank account. Pay yourself a salary. Do not dip into business money for personal expenses. If you do, you will never know if your business is profitable. Track your overheads. Overheads include transport, tools, insurance, rent, phone, internet, and administration. In Kenya, budget KES 15,000 per month for overheads if you are active. In Nigeria, NGN 150,000. In South Africa, ZAR 5,000. In Ghana, GHS 1,500. These costs must be covered by your project profits. If they are not, you are subsidising your business from your pocket. You will burn out. Build a team. You cannot scale alone. Hire a foreman who can run a site without you. Hire a driver if you do deliveries. Hire an accountant or bookkeeper part-time. In Kenya, a part-time bookkeeper costs KES 10,000 per month. In Nigeria, NGN 80,000. In South Africa, ZAR 3,000. In Ghana, GHS 800. This is worth it. A bookkeeper keeps your records clean and your taxes paid. Pay your taxes. In Kenya, register for VAT if your turnover exceeds KES 5 million per year. In Nigeria, register for VAT if turnover exceeds NGN 25 million. In South Africa, register for VAT if turnover exceeds ZAR 1 million. In Ghana, register for VAT if turnover exceeds GHS 200,000. Pay your taxes on time. Tax evasion destroys businesses. The taxman always catches up. Market your business. You need a brand. A name, a logo, a tagline. Print business cards. Create a WhatsApp Business profile. Post photos of your tanks. Ask for Google reviews. In Kenya, a Google Business profile is free. In Nigeria, use Facebook and Instagram. In South Africa, use Facebook Marketplace and Gumtree. In Ghana, use Jiji and Facebook. Attend local trade fairs and agricultural shows. Partner with NGOs and government agencies that build water projects. In Kenya, partner with the Ministry of Water and Sanitation. In Nigeria, partner with the Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Agency. In South Africa, partner with the Department of Water and Sanitation. In Ghana, partner with the Community Water and Sanitation Agency. These partnerships bring big contracts. Big contracts bring big profits. But big contracts also bring big risks. You need a contract. You need insurance. You need a cash flow plan. Never take a contract that is more than 30 percent of your annual turnover. If you do, one late payment will kill your business. Manage cash flow. Cash flow is the difference between money in and money out. You can be profitable on paper and still go broke if your clients pay late. Always ask for a deposit. Always invoice promptly. Always follow up on payments. If a client is late, stop work. Do not deliver the tank until you are paid. Keep a reserve of three months of overheads. In Kenya, that is KES 45,000. In Nigeria, NGN 450,000. In South Africa, ZAR 15,000. In Ghana, GHS 4,500. This reserve keeps you alive during slow months. Diversify your services. Do not only build tanks. Build gutters, soak pits, septic tanks, and greywater systems. Sell water filters. Offer tank cleaning and repair. Offer water testing. Each service adds revenue and keeps your crew busy. In Kenya, tank cleaning costs KES 5,000 per tank. In Nigeria, NGN 30,000. In South Africa, ZAR 1,000. In Ghana, GHS 300. Repair of cracks costs KES 8,000, NGN 50,000, ZAR 1,500, GHS 500. These are high-margin services. Train your workers. Send your foreman to a welding course. Send your masons to a waterproofing workshop. Send yourself to a business management course. In Kenya, a short course at a technical college costs KES 20,000. In Nigeria, NGN 100,000. In South Africa, ZAR 5,000. In Ghana, GHS 1,000. This investment pays for itself in better quality and faster work. Finally, think about legacy. Do you want to build tanks forever? Or do you want to build a company that builds tanks? A company has systems, people, and brand value. A company can be sold. A company can run without you. Start documenting your processes. Write down how you mix cement, how you tie mesh, how you cure concrete. Create a training manual. Use it to train new workers. This is how you scale from one tank at a time to ten tanks at a time. This is how you build wealth. This is how you build Africa.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Risk Management, Safety, and Quality Control in Water Tank Construction
lessons.body: Every water tank project carries risk. Risk of injury. Risk of material failure. Risk of non-payment. Risk of reputation damage. This lesson teaches you how to identify, manage, and reduce risk so your business survives and thrives. Start with safety. Water tank construction involves heavy materials, sharp tools, heights, and cement. The most common injuries are cuts from rebar, burns from cement, falls from walls, and back injuries from lifting. Prevent cuts by wearing leather gloves when handling rebar and mesh. Prevent burns by wearing long sleeves, gloves, and dust masks when mixing cement. Cement is caustic. It burns skin and eyes. If cement gets in the eye, rinse with clean water for 15 minutes and go to a clinic. Prevent falls by using scaffolding with guardrails. Never stand on the tank wall without a harness. Never use a ladder as a work platform. Ladders slip. Prevent back injuries by lifting with your legs, not your back. Use a wheelbarrow or a pulley to move heavy materials. Do not carry cement bags on your head. In Kenya, a back injury can cost KES 50,000 in medical bills and lost work. In Nigeria, NGN 300,000. In South Africa, ZAR 10,000. In Ghana, GHS 2,000. Safety is cheaper than injury. Provide clean drinking water on site. Heat stroke is common in hot climates. Provide shade. Rotate workers. Do not work during the hottest part of the day if you can avoid it. Start early. Finish before noon. Rest in the afternoon. Provide a first aid kit. Include bandages, antiseptic, burn gel, eye wash, and painkillers. Train one worker as a first aider. In Kenya, a first aid course costs KES 5,000. In Nigeria, NGN 30,000. In South Africa, ZAR 1,500. In Ghana, GHS 500. This is a small investment for a big reduction in risk. Now quality control. A leaking tank is a failed tank. A cracked tank is a failed tank. A tank that collapses is a disaster. Quality control starts with the foundation. The ground must be level and compacted. Use a plate compactor or a hand tamper. In Kenya, a plate compactor rental costs KES 3,000 per day. In Nigeria, NGN 20,000. In South Africa, ZAR 800. In Ghana, GHS 200. Compact in layers of 150mm. Water each layer. Do not build on soft ground. If the ground is soft, dig until you reach firm soil. Backfill with hardcore and compact. The foundation must be at least 100mm thick for a 10,000-litre tank. Use concrete with a ratio of 1 part cement to 2 parts sand to 4 parts aggregate. Add waterproofing admixture. Cure the foundation for at least 3 days before building walls. For ferrocement, the mesh must be tied tightly. Use binding wire every 150mm. Overlap mesh by 100mm. Do not leave gaps. Gaps cause cracks. The first coat of cement mortar should be 1 part cement to 3 parts sand. Apply it firmly. Push it into the mesh. Do not just smear it on. The second coat should be 1 part cement to 2 parts sand. Apply it after the first coat has set but is still green. Cure the tank for 7 days. Keep it wet. Cover it with a tarpaulin or plastic sheet. In Kenya, curing a 10,000-litre tank uses about 500 litres of water per day. In Nigeria, 600 litres. In South Africa, 400 litres. In Ghana, 500 litres. Water is cheap. Cracks are expensive. For concrete tanks, the formwork must be strong. It must not bulge or leak. Use timber or steel formwork. Brace it well. Vibrate the concrete to remove air pockets. Use a poker vibrator or tap the formwork with a hammer. Do not over-vibrate. Over-vibration causes segregation. Cure the concrete for 14 days. For brick tanks, the mortar must be 1 part cement to 4 parts sand. Fill every joint. Do not leave gaps. Render the inside with a waterproof render: 1 part cement to 2 parts sand plus waterproofing admixture. Render in two coats. Cure for 7 days. For plastic tanks, inspect for cracks before installation. Check the fittings. Use Teflon tape on threaded connections. Do not overtighten. Overtightening cracks plastic. Support the tank evenly. A plastic tank on uneven ground will crack. Use a concrete plinth or a sand bed. Now financial risk. The biggest financial risk is non-payment. Prevent it with a contract and a deposit. The second biggest risk is material price fluctuation. Prevent it with a price adjustment clause. The third biggest risk is project delay. Prevent it with a realistic timeline and a penalty clause for delays caused by the client. The fourth biggest risk is theft. Prevent it with secure storage and a night guard. In Kenya, a night guard costs KES 800 per night. In Nigeria, NGN 5,000. In South Africa, ZAR 300. In Ghana, GHS 100. The fifth biggest risk is reputation damage. Prevent it with quality work and honest communication. If you make a mistake, fix it. Do not blame the client. Do not hide. Word travels fast in African communities. A good reputation is your best marketing. A bad reputation is your worst enemy. Finally, review every project. After handover, sit with your team. What went well? What went wrong? What will you do differently next time? Write it down. Use it to improve your process. Use it to train new workers. Use it to price future projects. Risk management is not about avoiding all risk. It is about taking calculated risks and protecting yourself from the ones that can destroy you. Safety, quality, and honesty are your three pillars. Build on them, and your water tank business will stand strong for years.

SAFETY WARNING

Ferrocement and concrete tank construction involves silica dust, cement burns, and confined-space entry. Always wear N95 respirators when mixing dry cement, nitrile gloves when handling wet mortar, and never enter an empty tank deeper than 1.5 m without a harness, a second person outside, and forced ventilation. Cement dust is a respiratory sensitiser; wet cement causes alkali burns. In hot African climates (35-45 degrees C), schedule pours before 10:00 and after 16:00, and provide at least 1 litre of drinking water per worker per hour to prevent heat stroke.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Confirm client demand: litres per day = persons x 20 L (WHO basic) and size tank for at least 7 days storage.
  2. Lock material prices in writing before quoting; cement and steel can swing 15-25% in a single quarter in KES, NGN, GHS, and ZAR markets.
  3. Add 10% wastage for sand, ballast, and mesh; add 5% for cement bags lost to moisture or tearing.
  4. Price labour at 30-35% of total project cost; never quote below 25% or you will cut corners on curing.
  5. Include transport and last-mile delivery to rural sites; this is 8-12% of cost and the most common omission.
  6. Keep a written record of every bag, roll, and litre used per tank; variance above 8% signals theft or poor workmanship.
  7. Set aside 8-12% profit and a 5% contingency for weather delays, currency shifts, and client changes.
  8. Photograph every stage (foundation, mesh, render, curing) and file with the invoice for warranty and dispute protection.

Further Reading

  • FAO - Ferrocement Water Tanks: Design and Construction
  • WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene
  • WHO - Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality (4th edition)
  • Sphere Standards - Humanitarian Charter and Minimum Standards in Humanitarian Response
  • UNICEF - Water Supply Costing Tools and Rural Water Unit Costs

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a bill of quantities in water tank construction?
options: A) To list the labour rates only
B) To itemise materials, labour and costs for the project
C) To replace the construction drawing
D) To record weather conditions on site
quiz.explanation: A bill of quantities itemises materials, labour and associated costs so the project can be priced accurately.

quiz.q: Which cost is classified as a direct cost in water tank construction?
quiz.explanation: Cement and steel are materials consumed directly in building the tank, so they are direct costs.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an indirect cost on a water tank project?
quiz.explanation: Site supervision salaries support the whole project rather than a single work item, making them an indirect cost.

quiz.q: What does the term wastage allowance mean in material costing?
options: A) Extra quantity added to cover breakage and offcuts
B) Money refunded by the supplier
D) Discount given for bulk buying
quiz.explanation: A wastage allowance adds a percentage to the net quantity to cover breakage, offcuts and spillage.

quiz.q: Which document shows the expected cash flow over the duration of a tank project?
quiz.explanation: A cash flow forecast predicts money in and out over time, helping manage project liquidity.

quiz.q: Why is a contingency sum included in a water tank construction estimate?
options: B) To cover unforeseen costs and risks
C) To increase the profit margin only
D) To reduce the contract price
quiz.explanation: A contingency covers unforeseen events such as ground conditions or price increases.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a rate build-up in estimating?
options: A) To show how a unit rate is calculated from labour, material and plant
B) To list the names of workers
C) To record the daily site diary
D) To describe the tank dimensions
quiz.explanation: A rate build-up breaks a unit rate into its labour, material, plant and overhead components.

quiz.q: Which material is commonly used for the waterproof lining of potable water tanks?
options: B) Food grade epoxy or cement mortar
quiz.explanation: Food grade epoxy or cement mortar is safe for potable water and provides a durable waterproof lining.

quiz.q: What does the abbreviation OPC stand for in concrete works?
quiz.explanation: OPC stands for Ordinary Portland Cement, a common binder used in tank construction.

quiz.q: Which test is used to check the workability of fresh concrete?
quiz.explanation: The slump test measures the workability or consistency of fresh concrete.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of using precast concrete panels for water tanks?
options: B) They speed up construction and improve quality control
C) They eliminate the need for reinforcement
D) They are always cheaper than cast in situ
quiz.explanation: Precast panels are factory made, giving faster erection and better quality control.

quiz.q: Which factor most affects the cost of transporting materials to a remote site?
options: C) Number of workers on site
quiz.explanation: Distance and road conditions directly influence haulage time and transport charges.

quiz.q: What is a purchase order used for in construction procurement?
options: A) To formally request goods from a supplier
quiz.explanation: A purchase order is a formal document requesting a supplier to deliver specified goods.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a fixed cost for a construction company?
quiz.explanation: Monthly office rent does not change with project output, so it is a fixed cost.

quiz.q: What does value engineering aim to achieve in tank construction?
options: B) Reduce cost while maintaining function and quality
C) Replace all materials with cheaper substitutes
quiz.explanation: Value engineering seeks the best function at the lowest life cycle cost without sacrificing quality.

quiz.q: Which document records the actual materials delivered and used on site?
options: A) Store ledger or material register
quiz.explanation: A store ledger or material register tracks deliveries, issues and balances of materials.

quiz.q: In estimating, what is the unit of measurement for formwork?
quiz.explanation: Formwork is measured by area in square metres of contact surface.

quiz.q: Which of these is a renewable or recycled material option for tank construction?
quiz.explanation: Recycled steel reinforcement reduces environmental impact and is a sustainable option.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a retention sum in a construction contract?
options: A) To pay for extra work
B) To ensure defects are rectified after completion
quiz.explanation: Retention is money held back to ensure the contractor fixes defects during the defects liability period.

quiz.q: Which cost is likely to be the largest in a reinforced concrete water tank?
quiz.explanation: Concrete and reinforcement are the major structural materials and dominate the cost.

quiz.q: What does a break even analysis show a contractor?
options: A) The profit at maximum output
B) The point where income equals total cost
C) The number of workers needed
quiz.explanation: Break even analysis identifies the output level where total revenue equals total cost.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a source of finance for a small construction business?
quiz.explanation: A bank loan is a common external source of finance for small construction firms.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of buying materials at the lowest price without quality checks?
options: B) Poor quality leading to defects and rework
quiz.explanation: Cheap substandard materials often cause defects, rework and higher long term costs.

quiz.q: Which method helps control material theft on a water tank site?
options: B) Secure storage and stock records
quiz.explanation: Secure storage and accurate stock records reduce the risk of material theft.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a progress payment in construction?
options: A) Payment made for work completed to date
quiz.explanation: Progress payments are made periodically based on the value of work completed.

quiz.q: Which factor should be considered when selecting a water tank construction material?
options: B) Durability, cost and water quality safety
D) Brand of the contractor vehicle
quiz.explanation: Material selection must balance durability, cost and safety for potable water.

quiz.q: What does the term lead time mean in procurement?
options: A) Time taken to pour concrete
B) Time between placing an order and receiving goods
C) Time spent on site meetings
quiz.explanation: Lead time is the period from order placement to delivery of goods.

quiz.q: Which of these is a variable cost in tank construction?
options: B) Cement purchased per cubic metre poured
quiz.explanation: Cement cost varies with the volume of concrete poured, so it is a variable cost.

quiz.q: Why is accurate record keeping important for a construction business?
options: B) To track costs, manage cash flow and support claims
quiz.explanation: Accurate records help monitor costs, manage cash flow and support contractual claims.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of a joint venture for a small tank construction firm?
options: A) Sharing risks, resources and expertise on larger projects
quiz.explanation: A joint venture allows firms to pool resources and share risks on larger projects.
